questions.question: When should you use `path/filepath` instead of `path`?
questions.title: path/filepath versus path
questions.direct_answer: Use `path/filepath` for operating-system file paths because it follows the target platform's separator and volume rules. Use `path` for slash-separated logical paths such as URL path components and `io/fs` names. Neither package parses a complete URL; use `net/url` when schemes, hosts, queries, or escaping are involved.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `path` always treats slash as the separator.
Use filepath for local files and directories.
Use path for URL path components and slash-based logical names.
Use `net/url` for complete URLs, queries, and escaping.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`path/filepath` manipulates file names according to the target operating system. Separators, volumes, absolute-path rules, and cleaning therefore match the platform on which the program runs. It is the right package for paths passed to `os.Open` and other local filesystem calls.

`path` uses slash-separated paths on every operating system. That makes it suitable for URL path components, import-like names, archive entries, and `io/fs` paths whose contract defines slash rather than the host separator.

For example, `filepath.Join("reports", "today.csv")` creates a native local path. `path.Join("api", "v1", "users")` creates `api/v1/users` everywhere. Passing a full `https://` URL to path.Join is wrong because cleaning can alter the scheme separator.

Neither Join function validates that a path is authorised, exists, or stays inside a trusted directory. I choose the package from the path namespace, use `net/url` for complete URLs, and apply separate containment checks before using untrusted filesystem names.

sections.title: A path belongs to a namespace before it becomes a string
sections.content:
Local files, URL paths, and virtual filesystem names may look similar on Unix, but their separator and validity rules differ. Using the matching package makes that semantic choice explicit and preserves portability to Windows.

A full URL contains more than a path. Scheme, authority, query, fragment, and escaping require `net/url`. `path` is appropriate only after code is intentionally operating on the path component.

sections.title: Cleaning syntax is not parsing a resource identifier
sections.content:
Both Join functions clean redundant separators and dot elements within their own syntax. That convenience can be surprising when applied to a string containing a URL scheme or an untrusted traversal. Cleaning changes representation; it does not prove security or resource identity.

`filepath.Localize` can convert a valid slash-separated `io/fs` name to a native local path when that conversion is the intended boundary. It rejects names that cannot be represented safely on the target platform and returns a local path.

sections.title: Match the package to the namespace
sections.content:
| Value | Package | Separator contract |
|---|---|---|
| Local file name | `path/filepath` | Operating-system specific |
| URL path component | `path` | Slash on every platform |
| `io/fs` valid path | `path` or `filepath.Localize` at boundary | Slash in fs namespace |
| Complete URL | `net/url` | URL parsing and escaping rules |

sections.title: Build one filesystem path and one logical path
sections.content:
```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"path"
	"path/filepath"
)

func main() {
	local := filepath.Join("reports", "2026", "today.csv")
	logical := path.Join("api", "v1", "users")
	fmt.Println("local:", local)
	fmt.Println("logical:", logical)
}
```

questions.question: How do `filepath.Join`, `Clean`, `Base`, `Dir`, `Ext`, and `Rel` work?
questions.title: Core filepath operations
questions.direct_answer: `Join` combines elements with the native separator and cleans the result. `Clean` normalizes a path lexically. `Base` returns the last element, `Dir` everything before it, and `Ext` the final suffix beginning at the last dot in the last element. `Rel(base, target)` computes a lexical relative path whose join with base represents target.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `Join` combines elements and cleans the result.
`Clean` removes redundant separators and resolves dot elements lexically.
`Base` and `Dir` split the final element from its parent path.
`Ext` examines the suffix of the final path element.
`Rel` computes a relative representation, not an access-control decision.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`filepath.Join` joins elements with the operating system separator and returns a cleaned result. `Clean` performs lexical normalization: it removes repeated separators, eliminates dot elements, and resolves parent elements where possible. It does not access the filesystem.

`Base` returns the final element, while `Dir` returns the path excluding that final element in cleaned form. `Ext` returns the suffix beginning with the last dot in the final element, so `archive.tar.gz` has extension `.gz` rather than `.tar.gz`.

`Rel(base, target)` calculates a path that can represent target relative to base, provided the two can be related under platform rules. For example, from `workspace` to `workspace/reports/summary.csv` it returns `reports/summary.csv`.

These are lexical utilities. They do not prove that a path exists, resolve symbolic links, or show that a user is authorised to open it. In particular, Rel output can begin with `..`. I use these functions for representation and add an explicit security boundary for untrusted paths.

sections.title: Lexical operations reason about text under path rules
sections.content:
Filepath functions know platform syntax but normally do not consult directory entries. The same input text therefore produces a cleaned structure even when no corresponding file exists.

That distinction makes the utilities deterministic and fast, while leaving symlink resolution and permissions to explicit filesystem operations such as `EvalSymlinks`, `Stat`, or root-scoped open APIs.

sections.title: Name the unit returned by each function
sections.content:
Base and Dir are not guaranteed to return the original spelling because cleaning rules apply. Ext looks only within the last element. Rel can fail when paths cannot be made relative on a platform, and its result may escape through parent elements.

String-prefix checks are not a safe substitute for path-aware reasoning: `/srv/data2` begins with `/srv/data` as text but is not inside that directory. Use the containment tools designed for the boundary rather than composing utility outputs into an informal security check.

sections.title: One path through six operations
sections.content:
| Operation | Result for a reports path | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `Join("workspace", "reports", "summary.csv")` | Native combined path | Construct |
| `Clean` | Normalized spelling | Simplify lexically |
| `Base` | `summary.csv` | Final element |
| `Dir` | `workspace/reports` form | Parent portion |
| `Ext` | `.csv` | Final extension |
| `Rel("workspace", target)` | `reports/summary.csv` form | Relative representation |

questions.question: How do you keep an untrusted file path inside a trusted directory?
questions.title: Containing untrusted filesystem paths
questions.direct_answer: Reject absolute, empty, parent-escaping, and platform-reserved names with `filepath.IsLocal` before joining a lexical relative path to a base directory. That proves lexical containment only; symlinks can still escape. For actual untrusted file access on current Go, use `os.OpenRoot` or `os.OpenInRoot` so path traversal, including symlink traversal, is checked at the filesystem boundary.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Do not trust string-prefix checks for containment.
IsLocal does not account for symbolic links.
Use `os.OpenRoot` or `os.OpenInRoot` for symlink-aware confined access.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Untrusted file names must be treated as paths, not appended strings. `filepath.IsLocal(name)` rejects empty and absolute paths, parent traversal outside the evaluation directory, and reserved names on Windows. When it returns true, `filepath.Join(base, name)` is lexically contained within base.

Lexical containment is not complete filesystem containment. A path such as `reports/latest.txt` can pass IsLocal while `reports` is a symbolic link pointing outside the trusted tree. `Clean` and `Rel` cannot discover that because they do not walk filesystem links.

For example, an upload service can reject `../secret.txt` immediately. To read `reports/today.txt` safely on current Go, `os.OpenInRoot(base, name)` opens within a root and returns an error if a component refers outside it, including through traversal or symlinks, subject to the API's documented platform limitations.

The same boundary must cover creation, rename, and extraction, not only reads. I also authorise the logical resource, avoid user-controlled absolute bases, handle races through root-scoped operations, and run a maintained Go release because filesystem confinement is security-sensitive.

sections.title: Containment has a lexical layer and a filesystem layer
sections.content:
IsLocal answers a question about path syntax. It is useful for rejecting obvious traversal and for safely constructing display or lookup names beneath a base. It intentionally does not inspect directory entries.

Root-scoped open operations enforce the boundary while resolving the path. This closes the gap where a syntactically local component is a symlink to an external location and avoids fragile check-then-open sequences.

sections.title: Avoid security decisions based on prefixes
sections.content:
A string prefix cannot distinguish `/srv/data/file` from `/srv/data-old/file`, handle case and volume rules, or account for separators. A Rel-and-reject approach can establish lexical containment but still has the same symlink gap as IsLocal.

`os.OpenInRoot` was added in Go 1.24 and is equivalent to opening a root and then a name inside it. For several operations, keep an `os.Root` and use its methods. Read the current Root limitations and security advisories for the deployed Go version rather than treating any path helper as timeless sandboxing.

sections.title: Two containment checks
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Untrusted name] --> B{filepath.IsLocal?}
  B -- No --> C[Reject syntax]
  B -- Yes --> D[Lexically local name]
  D --> E[os.OpenInRoot base, name]
  E --> F{resolves inside root?}
  F -- No --> G[Reject traversal or symlink escape]
  F -- Yes --> H[Use opened file]
```
